name: Fork
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: When the Chain Splits in Two
lesson.summary: A fork is a point where a blockchain's history diverges into two or more competing versions, something that can happen briefly by accident or deliberately as a rule change.
lesson.body:
A blockchain, as defined earlier, is supposed to be a single agreed sequence of blocks. In practice, that single sequence occasionally splits, at least temporarily, into two or more competing versions that disagree about what happened next. That split is called a fork, and understanding why it happens is really an extension of the consensus mechanism chapter, since a fork is essentially consensus briefly failing to produce one clear answer.

The most common kind of fork is accidental and short lived. Because block production is happening across a network with real communication delay, two different miners or validators can produce two different, individually valid blocks at nearly the same moment, each building on the same previous block. Different nodes hear about these two candidate blocks in different order depending on network geography, and for a brief window, part of the network considers one block the latest and part considers the other. The chain has, technically, split into two competing branches.

Most consensus mechanisms include a built in way to resolve this without any human stepping in. On a proof of work chain, the rule is that nodes eventually follow whichever branch has accumulated the greatest total proof of work, often loosely called the longest chain rule even though it is really about cumulative work rather than block count alone. As soon as one branch pulls ahead by even one additional block, nodes still mining or building on the losing branch switch over, discard the blocks unique to that shorter branch in what is called a reorganization, and the network converges back to one agreed history. This kind of fork is usually resolved within one or two blocks and is a routine, expected part of how the network operates rather than a crisis.

A different kind of fork is deliberate rather than accidental: a change to the protocol's own rules. When developers want to add a feature or fix a flaw, they change what counts as a valid block, and every node has to decide whether to adopt the new rules. If the new rules are compatible enough that old, unupgraded nodes still accept blocks produced under them, the community stays on one chain even through the change. If the new rules are incompatible enough that old nodes reject blocks the new software considers valid, or the reverse, the network can split permanently into two separate chains with a shared history up to the fork point and different rules afterward, each now its own independent blockchain going forward.

Forks, in short, are not a single phenomenon but a spectrum, ranging from a routine few second hiccup resolved automatically by the consensus mechanism, to a deliberate, permanent rule change that can split a community as well as a chain. The next chapter looks closely at one specific, carefully designed category of deliberate fork, the soft fork, which is built specifically to avoid that kind of permanent split.
